title: Ethics in Psychological Research
in30Seconds: Research ethics are the rules that protect the people who take part in psychological studies and keep the science honest. The American Psychological Association's working standard is simple: participants must be treated fairly and without harm, and findings must be reported honestly. In practice that means informed consent before a study begins, strict limits on deception, a full debriefing when the study ends, confidentiality for every participant's data, and review-board approval before research with people can start.
whyItMatters: Psychology's findings are only as trustworthy as the way they were gathered. A study built on pressure, secrecy, or mistreatment produces knowledge no one should act on — which is why every serious psychology program teaches the rules before the methods. The same rules will follow you further than the classroom. If you ever read research to make a decision, you benefit from knowing participants were protected. If you ever design a study — even a small class project — you will be the one responsible for consent, disclosure, and confidentiality. And if you take part in research yourself, as many students do, the rules describe your rights: what you should be told, what you can refuse, and what must happen before you leave.
learningObjectives: Define research ethics and state the APA's working standard: participants must be treated fairly and without harm, and findings must be reported honestly.
Explain informed consent as a participant's voluntary agreement based on understanding, including the right to decline or withdraw at any time.
Describe when deception is allowed in research and why participants who were deceived must receive a full debriefing afterward.
Identify what an institutional review board (IRB) does and why its approval is required before research with human participants proceeds.
Analyze the historical cases — the Tuskegee syphilis study and Milgram's obedience research — that shaped today's ethics rules, and apply the rules to an original research scenario.

collegeVersion.heading: What research ethics are
collegeVersion.body: Research ethics are the values, principles, and standards that guide how studies are designed, carried out, and reported. The APA Dictionary of Psychology defines them exactly that way, and its entry on ethics makes the standard concrete for research: participants must be treated fairly and without harm, and investigators must report results and findings honestly. Honest reporting matters as much as fair treatment: invented or hidden findings corrupt the knowledge everyone else builds on. The APA's Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct turns the same commitments into a working professional code, and the APA Dictionary notes that research ethics require studies with human participants to be evaluated by an institutional review board. The working definition for this lesson is the APA's: treat participants fairly and without harm, and report honestly.

collegeVersion.heading: Informed consent
collegeVersion.body: Informed consent is a participant's voluntary agreement to take part, given with real understanding of what the study involves. The APA Dictionary defines it as voluntary agreement based on understanding of a procedure's nature, its potential benefits and possible risks, and the available alternatives, and it notes that participants are free to decline or to withdraw at any time. The U.S. Office for Human Research Protections describes the same idea in three moves: researchers must disclose the information needed for an informed decision, make sure participants understand it, and protect voluntariness so that no one is coerced or unduly influenced. In practice, consent is documented with a signed form before the study starts, describing what participation involves, noting risks, and stating that involvement is voluntary and can be discontinued without penalty. An original example: a researcher recruiting for a study on study habits must tell participants how long the session runs and what they will be asked to do, and they can leave at any moment with no consequence. A signature from someone rushed, pressured, or misled is not informed consent — it is paperwork.

collegeVersion.heading: Deception and debriefing
collegeVersion.body: Deception is any distortion or withholding of fact with the purpose of misleading others. The APA Dictionary's example is the classic case: not disclosing the true purpose of an experiment to a participant. Sometimes deception is necessary, because participants who know the exact question may change their behavior and ruin the results — OpenStax's example is a researcher concealing an interest in how clothing affects opinions. But deception is tightly bounded: never harmful, and when a study uses it, participants must receive a full debriefing — complete, honest information about the purpose, how the data will be used, and why the deception was necessary. The APA Dictionary defines debriefing as giving participants in a completed research project a fuller explanation of the study than was possible before or during the research. The best-known historical example is Stanley Milgram's obedience research at Yale in 1963: 40 men were led to believe they were taking part in a study to improve learning and memory and told to deliver electric shocks — in 15-volt steps up to 450 volts — to a learner whenever the learner erred. The learners were confederates who never received shocks, and 65% of participants continued to the maximum voltage. Participants were deceived about the true purpose — the real question was obedience to authority — which is why the study is taught in ethics discussions as the standard example of deception and why disclosure afterward is a rule, not a courtesy.

collegeVersion.heading: Confidentiality
collegeVersion.body: Confidentiality protects the information participants reveal in confidence. The APA Dictionary describes it as a professional-ethics principle shielding research participants and survey respondents against unauthorized access to what they share, and OpenStax notes that the consent form guarantees collected data remain completely confidential. In practice, answers, scores, and identifying details are stored and reported so no unauthorized person can link them to the person who gave them. An original example: in a study of stress among first-year students, the researcher may know who said what, but the published paper reports only group patterns and the raw data stay in locked files. Confidentiality is what makes honest answers possible; people will not tell the truth about sensitive topics if their identities can leak.

collegeVersion.heading: The review board — and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Before research with human participants can proceed, it must pass through an institutional review board (IRB). The APA Dictionary calls the IRB a committee that reviews research proposals for ethical acceptability; it helps protect participants and is mandatory at any U.S. institution receiving federal funds for research. OpenStax adds that its approval is generally required before an experiment can proceed. The honest framing: these rules exist because people were hurt before the rules did. In the Tuskegee syphilis study, the U.S. Public Health Service recruited rural Black men in Tuskegee, Alabama, in 1932, promising free medical care, meals, and burial insurance; 600 men took part. Those who tested positive for syphilis were never told they had it, penicillin was withheld even after it became a recognized treatment in 1947, and the study ran for 40 years — ending in 1972 only after the national press exposed it. The outrage led to the National Research Act of 1974 and to today's strict guidelines, and the Belmont Report of 1979 distilled three principles — respect for persons, beneficence, and justice — that still anchor U.S. oversight of human-subjects research. Milgram's study is part of the same history: a landmark finding about obedience, and a reminder of what deception looks like and why the rules require full disclosure afterward.

vocabulary.definition: The values, principles, and standards that guide researchers in designing studies, carrying them out, and reporting findings (APA Dictionary of Psychology).
A participant's voluntary agreement to take part in a study, based on understanding its nature, risks, and benefits; participants may decline or withdraw at any time.
Misleading participants or withholding information about a study, typically its true purpose; allowed only when necessary for valid results and never harmful.
The fuller explanation of a study given to participants after it is complete, covering the true purpose and how the data will be used.
Protecting the information participants share in confidence from unauthorized access or disclosure.
A committee that reviews research proposals involving human participants for ethical acceptability before the research can proceed.
Done by free choice; participation in research is always voluntary, and participants can withdraw without penalty.
To leave a study at any time without penalty; the right to withdraw is part of informed consent.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Research ethics are the rules that keep studies with people honest and safe. Before a study starts, participants must be told what they are agreeing to, and they can say no or walk away at any time — that is informed consent. Some studies need to hide part of their purpose, because knowing it would change how people behave; that is deception, and it is only allowed when it does not hurt anyone. When the study ends, the researcher must explain the true purpose — that is debriefing. Personal data stay protected — that is confidentiality. And none of it starts until a review board says yes. In one line: tell people what they are in for, do not hurt them, come clean afterward, and protect their information.
eli10.analogy: Think of a research participant as a house guest. A good host says what is for dinner before anyone sits down (informed consent), does not film the guest through a hidden camera (no secret data collection), and thanks them at the door with the full story of the evening (debriefing). The guest came freely and can leave whenever they like.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down because a guest can spot a bad host and walk out, while a participant often cannot tell how much is being kept from them — deception is hidden by design. So research leans on formal safeguards: a review board that approves the study in advance, written rules, and mandatory disclosure afterward. Good manners protect guests; rules protect participants.

workedExample: Designing a study with deception, the right way. Maya wants to study whether people judge a speaker's honesty differently when the speaker breaks eye contact. If she announces the real question, participants will watch the speaker's eyes on purpose, and her results will be meaningless. So she proposes deception: participants will be told the study is about how well people remember spoken information. Before anything happens, her university's IRB must approve the plan. At recruitment, participants get an honest consent form covering the session, the risks (none beyond ordinary conversation), and the right to withdraw at any time. During the study, the deception touches only the stated purpose — nothing harmful. Afterward, every participant is debriefed: told the true purpose, why it was hidden, and how the data will be used. Their responses stay confidential.

commonMistakes.mistake: Informed consent is just getting a signature.
commonMistakes.correction: The signature documents consent; the consent itself is the participant's voluntary agreement based on understanding. A form signed by someone who was rushed, pressured, or misled gives the researcher paperwork, not informed consent — the APA Dictionary defines consent by understanding and voluntariness, not by ink.

commonMistakes.mistake: Deception is never allowed in research.
commonMistakes.correction: Deception is allowed when it is necessary to protect the integrity of the results and it causes no harm — but participants must receive a full debriefing afterward (OpenStax Psychology 2e). The rule bans harmful or unnecessary deception, not all concealment of purpose.

commonMistakes.mistake: Consent and debriefing are the same conversation, just at different times.
commonMistakes.correction: They are different acts with different content. Consent happens before the study: agreeing to take part with understanding of what it involves. Debriefing happens after: a fuller explanation of the study — especially the true purpose and why deception was used — owed to every participant once the research is complete (APA Dictionary).

commonMistakes.mistake: A study with no physical risk needs no review board.
commonMistakes.correction: The IRB weighs ethics, not just physical danger. At any U.S. institution receiving federal research funds, an IRB is mandatory, and it reviews proposals involving human participants — including surveys and studies whose only risks are psychological or social — before the research proceeds (APA Dictionary; OpenStax).

compareContrast.distinction: Consent comes before the study: the participant agrees to take part with understanding of what it involves. Debriefing comes after: the fuller explanation of the study — especially the true purpose — that participants are owed once the research is complete.

Deception withholds or distorts specific information, typically the study's purpose, to keep results valid — and it is bounded: never harmful, always disclosed in the debriefing. A lie about risks or about what participants will experience crosses the line because it destroys the understanding that informed consent depends on.

Research ethics are field-specific rules that govern how studies are designed, run, and reported (APA Dictionary). Moral philosophy asks broader questions about what is right and wrong in general — a separate discipline that this lesson does not attempt to cover.

keyTakeaway: Research ethics protect the people who make psychology possible: every participant is a volunteer who must be treated fairly and without harm, informed before the study, and fully explained to afterward — because people were hurt before these rules existed.

questionBank.prompt: During recruitment for a study on sleep habits, a researcher tells potential participants that they may leave the study at any time, even after signing the form. Which principle is the researcher honoring?
options: Debriefing
The right to withdraw, which is part of informed consent
Confidentiality
Deception
questionBank.explanation: The APA Dictionary defines informed consent as voluntary agreement in which participants are free to decline or withdraw from the research at any time, so the promise reflects informed consent. Debriefing is the explanation given after the study, confidentiality protects data, and deception means misleading participants.
questionBank.skill: Recalling that informed consent includes the right to withdraw at any time

questionBank.prompt: A study used deception because telling participants the true purpose would have changed their behavior. What must the researcher do when the study ends?
options: Nothing, because the participants signed consent forms
Erase all records so participants cannot be identified
Provide a full debriefing: the true purpose, why the deception was necessary, and how the data will be used
Ask participants to sign a second consent form for the deception
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax Psychology 2e states that when deception is involved, participants must receive a full debriefing upon conclusion — complete, honest information about the purpose, why the deception was necessary, and how the data will be used. The other options skip the required disclosure.
questionBank.skill: Recalling that deception requires a full debriefing after the study

questionBank.prompt: Priya wants to study how people react to being left out of a group. She plans to tell participants they are playing a strategy game and to reveal the real purpose only at the end. Which condition must her study meet for that deception to be acceptable?
options: Participants must never learn the true purpose, so the results stay clean
The deception must continue after the study ends, to protect other participants
The deception must replace informed consent entirely
The deception must not be harmful, and participants must receive a full debriefing afterward
questionBank.explanation: Deception is permitted only when it is necessary to keep results valid, must not be harmful, and must be followed by a full debriefing in which the true purpose is disclosed (OpenStax Psychology 2e; APA Dictionary). The other options describe permanent concealment, which the rules do not allow.
questionBank.skill: Applying the rules that bound deception in research to a new scenario

questionBank.prompt: A critic claims researchers can police their own ethics and that formal oversight is unnecessary. Which historical case most directly refutes that claim?
options: The Tuskegee syphilis study, in which the U.S. Public Health Service withheld treatment from men who were never told they had the disease, until the press exposed it in 1972
The Asch conformity studies, in which participants judged the lengths of lines
Milgram's obedience study, in which participants believed they were delivering shocks to a learner
Ebbinghaus's memory experiments, in which he tested himself on nonsense syllables
questionBank.explanation: Tuskegee is the case where researchers inside a respected institution caused decades of harm with no effective internal check — the study ended only when the national press exposed it in 1972, and the outrage led to the National Research Act of 1974 (OpenStax Psychology 2e). The other studies are famous for different findings and do not show that same failure of self-policing.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing historical cases as evidence for why research oversight exists

questionBank.prompt: A university that receives federal research funding wants to run a short, no-risk survey about students' study habits. No deception is involved. Which of the following still applies under the rules in this lesson?
options: Nothing — a study with no risk needs no oversight
The proposal still needs IRB review, and participants still give informed consent, with their data kept confidential
The researcher may skip consent but must debrief participants afterward
The IRB must approve the survey, but once it starts, participants may not withdraw
questionBank.explanation: An institutional review board is mandatory at any U.S. institution receiving federal funds for research, informed consent applies to participation in research generally, and consent documents guarantee confidentiality (APA Dictionary; OpenStax). None of the other options matches those requirements.
questionBank.skill: Applying IRB, consent, and confidentiality rules to a low-risk study

provenance.rightsStatus: Reference-only synthesis. APA Dictionary of Psychology entries are copyrighted and were paraphrased, never reproduced; OpenStax Psychology 2e (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) used as reference with facts restated in original wording, and OpenStax's no-LLM-ingestion notice was respected. OHRP informed-consent FAQs and the Belmont Report are U.S. government works. The APA Ethics Code PDF is copyrighted, reference-only. All examples, scenarios, analogies, and practice questions are original to this lesson.
provenance.transformation: Working definition of research ethics (participants treated fairly and without harm; honest reporting) synthesized from the APA Dictionary of Psychology entries 'ethics' and 'research ethics'; informed consent from the APA Dictionary entry and OHRP's informed-consent FAQ; deception and debriefing from the APA Dictionary entries and OpenStax Psychology 2e section 2.4; confidentiality from the APA Dictionary entry and OpenStax; the IRB from the APA Dictionary entry and OpenStax; Milgram's study described factually from OpenStax section 12.4 and used as the historical deception example; the Tuskegee account and its link to the National Research Act of 1974 from OpenStax 2.4, with the Belmont Report's three principles from the registered Belmont Report record. All worked examples, scenarios, and questions are original.
